Just looking at the setup screen, I knew I wasn't going to Mint this. I was not wrong!

posts.name: LewdDolphin21
posts.cooked:
I Minted, with Bunker incapaciated, the others in single digits. Bunker got incapacitated because I miscalculated an External Combustion on the penultimate round. It was an unnecessary play anyway, but Citizen Dare was in play and I took the dare. :P

A few things to note:

  1. Chastise can help with getting Zealous Offense out later. That 2 points of self-damage counts towards the 3-damage condition, and allows for one of the damaging Citizens to be neutered for a bit.
  2. Other than End of Days, the first hero to be able to destroy Return with the Dawn is, somewhat ironically, Bunker. Destroy it when you can.
  3. Velociraptors are your friends. Let them eat the Citizens for you!
  4. Infrared Eyepiece should be played and used as soon as you get it. When exactly you get it comes down to deck shuffles--I had played Impromptu Invention at some point to get Utility Belt into play, so it might be possible you won't see it. However, a certain nasty card is somewhat buried in her deck, so you have quite a bit of time to worry about it.
  5. Try to prioritize damage on Dawn, especially once both Obsidian Fields are in play. Fanatic's Zealous Offense helps stop Citizens from harming you, anyway (outside of Tears, of course).
  6. Since H=3 in this game, Citizen Dawn flips back to her front side if there are 2 Citizens in play. Since Dawn is herself a Citizen, this means you need only one other Citizen in play to flip her back. Thus you can get it set up so she flips and flips back immediately, allowing you to destroy all future Citizens indiscriminately. (E.g., if there are 4 Citizens in the trash, and Dawn and 2 other Citizens in play, you can have a Velociraptor eat one Citizen, and then on Dawn's turn she will flip and flip back.)

posts.name: schadkehnfreude
posts.cooked:
I'm not going to say this one-shot is a slam dunk but it's definitely mintable without doing things that defy common sense/logic.  My recall is hazy but I only skip/skipped once, with Fanatic since I didn't have a better play to get around Truth's -1 damage resist.

Bottom line is that this is a damage race and you are absolutely given the tools to win it, if not much more than that.  On one hand, yes you're saddled with a pretty bad opening salvo of citizens and only have 3 heroes on your team.  On the other hand, one of them is Wraith who is arguably the single best hero to take to a Dawn fight and the other two will absolutely put in big time work for you as well.  Not gonna say anymore since I've probably already spoilered too much, but reading through it looks like other people also one-shot this doing different things than I did so there are multiple paths to victory

posts.name: robb8888
posts.cooked:
Powerhound_2000:

MigrantP with all the B.S. apparently. 

 

Look, all I'm saying is that for all of these One-Shots, I run several test games first, getting used to how the heroes interact with the villain, the environment, and each other; keeping track of the major pitfalls to be wary of; and the like.  (In this particular game, I played until I beat Dawn 3 times in a row, at which point I figured it was time to try the actual scenario.)  When I get to a point that I'm pretty comfortable that I have a good strategy to beat it, I play the One-Shot for real…

 

…and invariably come across some strange combination of cards/bad draws that never came up (or even close to came up) in my practice games, which (a) give all of the heroes awful draws; (b) give the villains completely insane/impractical draws; (c) completely neuter one of the heroes; (d) disincentivize otherwise completely sensible plays that most people would make (like in this game, getting out Flak Cannon/Razor Ordinance) and/or (e) render all of the strategies and gambits from the practice games, or other "conventional" plays, completely useless.  

 

So I play the scenario over and over and over again, losing and losing and losing again, trying different things until I happen on the one combination of plays/moves that manages to beat it.   And quite often it is one combination, there's no room for error; playing one card differently makes the difference between winning and losing.   And I think, "Well, it wasn't unbeatable," but also "But how in the heck was I supposed to stumble upon that particular combination of moves/plays on the very first try, with no 'undo's?"   

 

Then I read stuff on the boards along the lines of, "Oh, yeah - I Minted by skipping all of the heroes' first two turns…," or "I Minted by having Argent Adept be my main damage dealer," or "I Minted by using nothing but Wrathful Gaze…," or other moves that defy convention.  My reactions tend to be along the lines of:  (1) "So…beating this setup requires doing something out of the ordinary."  (2) "But how do you know you have to play out-of-the ordinary without playing it and losing, therefore not getting Mint?"   

 
Is the whole point of these things just to assume that the strategies one would normally employ won't work, and to start every game by experimenting with something bizarre, hoping that first time you'll luck upon the unusual combination that will get past the bad draws/bad deck lineup?
